rationale: A wins because it is more disciplined: three real reporter shapes, each with a beat, a reason to write now, and proof gates that would survive first contact with an editor. It still soils the carpet with “Oatly wins its biggest pour-volume deal,” which is not in the facts, but the underlying plant-closure-versus-distribution tension is usable. B has a terrific data headline in “What did the audit count?” and then starts freelancing with “Oatly launches its lowest-footprint product,” which is a flatly unsupported superlative.
gaps_in_A: “Oatly wins its biggest pour-volume deal” invents a superlative. The update says 1,400 locations, not Oatly’s biggest deal.
“same quarter it closes a US plant” is shakier than the supplied facts. The update supports same window, not necessarily same quarter.

“The retail angle: what no price change means for shoppers” is dismissed too hard. No price change is thin alone, but tied to a verified footprint cut it could support a green-premium or margin question if proof exists.
The chain angle lists “no price change at retail” under facts it rests on, but retail pricing does not prove the foodservice default story.
gaps_in_B: “Oatly launches its lowest-footprint product” is invented. The facts only say 31% lower than the previous formula.
“Oatly’s greener oat milk costs the same at the shelf” is a clever angle, but it leans on an external green-premium premise the update does not supply.
“category correction” overreaches. One unprofitable company closing one plant is not category evidence without comps.
“Next step: journalist-fit-check” is premature. The chain, LCA firm, plant, headcount, and price claim need fact-checking before names get pulled.
